newsitem.title: USA: Clinton seeks to lay ground for European security.
newsitem.headline: Clinton seeks to lay ground for European security.

text.p: To hear his supporters tell it, President Bill Clinton visits western Europe this week to celebrate its half century of peace since World War Two and to lay the groundwork for the entire continent's future security.

To hear his detractors, the president's plan to sign a Russia-NATO charter in Paris on Tuesday, paving the way to the security alliance's likely expansion into Eastern Europe, may instead breed instability.

Clinton leaves Washington on Monday, travelling first to Paris where he will meet Russian President Boris Yeltsin to sign the NATO-Russia Founding Act that will formally link the North Atlantic Treaty Organisation with its one-time enemy.

He visits the Netherlands on Wednesday to mark the 50th anniversary of the Marshall Plan, the U.S.-funded programme that helped rebuild western Europe after the war, and on Thursday he calls on new British Prime Minister Tony Blair in London.

In Clinton's view the NATO-Russia pact, and the expansion of NATO into Eastern Europe it is designed to bring about, may prevent a recurrence of the wars that have scarred the last two centuries of European history.

"We have had a long Cold War, and two world wars in the 20th century, and a 19th century full of heartache and bloodshed because people were arguing over territory in Europe," Clinton told reporters last week.
"We now have a chance to create a European continent where nation states for the first time say they are going to respect each others' borders and work together on common security problems," he said.

"To find a framework which accomplishes that and which also keeps the United States ... tied to the security and the freedom and the territorial integrity of Europe is an extraordinary achievement and it gives us a chance to write a whole new chapter in the 21st century," he said.
His critics took a very different view.

"NATO can continue to seve a useful role in European security only if it does not keep the Russians out," Raymond Garthoff, foreign policy analyst at the Brookings Institution, wrote in the spring issue of Brookings Review.

"We should have learned that no one gains security by creating insecurity for others. If legitimate Russian security interests are not met, neither will the long run interests of Eastern Europe, the United States and the world," he said.

Simply stated, the Russia-NATO act aimed to offer Russia a voice in NATO's deliberations and to allay its concerns about the alliance's eastward advance, bringing closer to its borders those states backed by NATO's military muscle.
NATO is expected in July to invite the Czech Republic, Hungary and Poland to become members, a development that Russia opposed but reluctantly accepted.
Russia would win a closer relationship to the alliance through the new agreement, which would create a NATO-Russia Joint Council in which it would have veto power.
But the alliance's governing body, the North Atlantic Council, would continue to set NATO policy, rendering Russia's veto within the other council effectively meaningless.

U.S. officials argue that the gradual rapprochment of NATO with the Eastern European countries that once made up its Warsaw Pact foes, without undermining Russia, is the only way to achieve lasting stability on the continent.

"If those contries were to be consigned to a limbo or a gray zone between the old Soviet Union and the old NATO, and the old NATO were to be frozen in amber, a number of things that would be bad would be likely to happen," Deputy Secretary of State Strobe Talbott told reporters last week.

"Those countries would be very likely to kind of scramble around ... to develop their own security arrangements in a way that would pit them against each other and also end up with much higher levels of military spending," he said.

"You have to do this in a way that both enlarges NATO and does not undermine the security or create second-class members on the one hand, and on the other, does not undermine Russian democracy," said National Security Adviser Sandy Berger. "What's been proven over the last year of very painstaking work -- the last two or three -- is that that's possible."
